title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 321
paragraphs: The pillars which Sesostris of Egypt set up in the various countries are for the most part no longer to be seen extant; but in Syrian Palestine I myself saw them existing, with the inscription I have mentioned and the emblem carved upon them. Moreover, in Ionia there are two figures of this man carved upon rocks — one on the road by which one goes from the land of Ephesus to Phocaea, and the other on the road from Sardis to Smyrna. In each place there is a figure of a man cut in the rock, of four cubits and a span in height, holding in his right hand a spear and in his left a bow and arrows, with similar equipment elsewhere, being both Egyptian and Ethiopian in character; and from the one shoulder to the other across the breast runs an inscription carved in sacred Egyptian characters, saying thus: “This land with my own shoulders I won for myself.” But who he is and from where, he does not declare in these places, though in other places he has declared this. Some of those who have seen these carvings conjecture that the figure is that of Memnon; but in this they are very far from the truth.
